newsitem.title: USA: U.S. must never default on its debt - Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. must never default on its debt - Greenspan.

text.p: Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Monday the United States must never default on its debt, adding that even a "whiff" of such an event would have serious repercussions for years to come.
Speaking to the Public Securities Association (PSA) here, Greenspan recounted the changes in the marketplace and government since the first Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton was in office.
"It is inevitable that consideration of the budget be included as part of a wider debate on public policies," Greenspan said in his remarks.
"However Alexander Hamilton drew a line that no one should cross: the government of the United States must never default on its debt," Greenspan added.
The Fed chief said even a "whiff" of the possibility that the United States would not honour its financial commitments "would push up the cost of borrowing for years to come."

Last year, wranglings over the federal budget and a standoff on raising the debt ceiling prompted Moody's Investors Sevice Inc and IBCA to put a portion of the U.S. debt on review for possible downgrade.
Moody's is one of the largest U.S. credit rating agencies, and IBCA is the European credit rating agency.
Standard and Poor's, the other major U.S. credit agency, kept close tabs on the budget and debt ceiling situations, but never actually put any U.S. debt on review.
Greenspan said policymakers at the Federal Reserve will do their part "to contribute to financial stability, which is to preserve the purchasing power of money over time."

The Fed Chairman received the PSA's 1996 Distinguished Public Service Award at its annual awards dinner here. The award is given to recognise the accomplishments of individuals who have had significant impact on the public securities business at the federal, state and local level.
